tier_reason: README 'Current C2MIR Performance Data' table states i5-13600K, FC37, GCC 12.3.1 and shows c2m -O2 -eg compile 336us vs gcc -O2 27.1ms (80x) and gcc -O0 26.1ms (77x). The sieve source (sieve.c) and a c2m-only timing target (GNUmakefile c2mir-sieve-bench) are public, but no script times the gcc side of the compile comparison (c-benchmarks/run-benchmarks.sh times execution only), so it falls short of A. First-party numbers with partial methodology = C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.3.1 -O2 and -O0 (gcc run on a memory filesystem); c2m -O2 -eg (generator) and c2m -ei (interpreter)
corrections.caveats: Project's own README table (first-party). The headline baseline is gcc -O2 (80x); the gcc -O0 column (77x) is extra context, and for compile time -O0 is gcc's fastest setting, so the -O0 cap does not drive the tier. What keeps it at C is that the gcc compile timing is not scripted in the repo. The workload is one tiny function with no #include files, and gcc runs on a memory filesystem. That is a best case for a minimal front-end and not typical of multi-file, header-heavy C builds. On the same table, c2m-generated code runs at about 92% of gcc -O2 speed on sieve (1.74s vs 1.6s) and at 0.91 geomean over 15 c-benchmarks.

notes: Numbers match the page exactly. The tier stays C, but the record's caveat wrongly said the -O0 column caps it; I rewrote that caveat. Metadata checked: MIT, 2658 stars, last commit 2026-06-19, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: bellard.org/tcc gives a first-party table: TinyCC 0.9.22 2.27s (859000 lines/s, 29.6 MB/s) vs GCC 3.2 -O0 20.0s (98000 lines/s, 3.4 MB/s) on a 2.4 GHz Pentium 4. No benchmark script is published, and the baseline is gcc -O0, so it is C.

corrections.workload: Compiling the Links web browser from source: 76,936 lines including headers, but 1,950,947 lines (67.2 MB) are actually compiled because the same headers are included in many files. Time covers compilation, assembly and linking (real time).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 3038 stars (unofficial GitHub mirror of the repo.or.cz mob branch); the V language bundles TCC binaries for fast development builds

notes: The record misread the page: 76,936 is the line count including headers, and 1,950,947 is the number of lines compiled. The speedup and timing numbers match the page. I removed the unsupported 'QEMU TCG lineage' usage claim: QEMU's docs say only that TCG 'began as a generic backend for a C compiler', not that it uses TinyCC. Metadata checked: LGPL-2.1, 3038 stars, last commit 2026-09-22.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. In his Nov 2024 progress report, the maintainer (bjorn3) says that on the rustc-perf suite, after lld was enabled for non-LLVM backends, 'most benchmarks [were] 10-50% faster' than cg_llvm. Issue #878 (2020) gives debug-build figures of about 10-60% (often about 40%) with the rustc-perf patch. Both are first-party numbers without hardware or version details, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: rustc-perf wall time, cg_clif vs cg_llvm (Nov 2024 nightly, after rustc allowed lld with non-LLVM backends): 'most benchmarks being 10-50% faster'; a couple of secondary (pathological) benchmarks still regressed. Earlier 2020 run (issue #878, debug profile): clean and baseline-incremental builds about 10-60% faster (often about 40%), but clean-incremental builds much slower (up to about 200%) because object files were not cached.
corrections.caveats: First-party figures only, read from blog/issue prose. The underlying result tables are images, and no hardware, nightly version or raw data are given. The Nov 2024 report does not state the build profile, though cg_clif targets debug builds. Issue #878's 2020 numbers are stale, and there the maintainer points to the Nov 2024 report as the latest results. Regressions remain on some stress-test benchmarks, and slower linking dominated some 2020 results. Release/optimized builds are not a target.

notes: Numbers do exist: issue #878 has them in its body text, and the maintainer's Nov 2024 progress report (linked from #878 as 'latest results') has more. So the tier moves from D to C, and benchmark_url is set to that report. The repo is dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0 (LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE, and the README says so); GitHub shows only Apache-2.0. Other metadata checked: 2141 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, and the README confirms the rustup rustc-codegen-cranelift-preview component.

tier_reason: The README at fdf8555f gives only rounded figures (~25x Prettier, ~15x ESLint on an M1 MacBook Pro), with no raw output and no tool versions. History shows these figures are the Nov 2022 Rome-era results (commit ec1feb472a, text renamed Rome->Biome) and were never re-measured. The cited commit's benchmark/bench.js is a 2024 rewrite with 2026 dependency pins that disables parallel-prettier, so the public code does not reproduce the stated numbers. That makes them first-party numbers with partial methodology: C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Formatting: ~25x faster than Prettier, ~20x faster than parallel-prettier and than xargs -P prettier, 1.5 to 2x faster than dprint, single-threaded ~7x faster than Prettier; '100 times faster than Prettier on an M1 Max with 10 cores'. Linting: ~15x faster than ESLint (without plugins), single-threaded ~4x. These were measured on Rome, Biome's predecessor, in Nov 2022.
corrections.workload: Wall time of formatting (Prettier, dprint) and linting (ESLint, only rules both tools support, no type-aware rules) on real JS/TS repos cloned by benchmark/bench.js (webpack, prettier and eslint sources). Formatting runs on already-formatted files after 2 hyperfine warmups. The published numbers come from the 2022 Rome-era run on target/webpack.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark/ directory was removed from main in 8e4ada5 ('chore: remove benchmark from repository', #10355, 2026-05-13). fdf8555f (2026-04-27, a dprint bump) is the last commit that touched benchmark/, and its README matches the removal commit's parent. The numbers are Nov 2022 Rome measurements, rounded and never re-run. At the cited commit, bench.js has parallel-prettier commented out ('crashing on Node 22') and pins eslint 9.39.4, prettier 3.8.3 and dprint 0.54.0, so the code does not reproduce the stated setup. The biomejs.dev homepage now claims '~35x faster than Prettier when formatting 171,127 lines of code in 2,104 files with an Intel Core i7 1270P', but it links to tree/main/benchmark, which no longer exists.

notes: Downgraded from A to C because the published numbers are stale, rounded Rome-era (2022) figures not produced by the cited code. The homepage's ~35x (i7-1270P) claim may have its own source worth tracking down in enrichment. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0 (spdx; benchmark package.json says MIT OR Apache-2.0), 25853 stars, last commit 2026-09-24.

tier_reason: oxc-project/bench-linter publishes the harness (bench-vscode/bench.sh, bench-vue, bench-sentry: hyperfine -w 1 -i with the oxlint/eslint command lines and configs). The README shows raw hyperfine output against ESLint v9 with each machine named (M2 Max 12-core, M4 Max, M3 Air 8-core). Code, configuration and CPU are all stated, so A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README summary: 'Oxlint is 50x - 100x faster than ESLint depending on the number of CPU cores' and '~2x faster than Biome'. VS Code, standard rules, vs ESLint v9: 62.10x (M2 Max 12-core), 118.25x (M4 Max), 60.09x (M3 Air 8-core); single-threaded Oxlint is ~17x faster than ESLint on M2 Max (derived from page data: 31.025s / 1.824s). Vs Biome (VS Code; bench.sh uses a single no-debugger rule): 2.72x, 2.49x, 3.31x. Type-aware rules vs typescript-eslint (M2 Max): 8.22x on Vue core, 12.38x on Sentry.
corrections.workload: Linting the VS Code src tree with standard rules (the Biome comparison uses only the no-debugger rule), plus Vue core and Sentry with type-aware rules vs typescript-eslint. Timed with hyperfine (1 warmup, non-zero exits ignored), with no ESLint cache.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: hyperfine -w 1 -i; oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json (plus a --threads=1 run) vs eslint -c eslint.config.mjs (ESLint v9 per README); prebuilt npm binaries, exact versions pinned only in pnpm-lock
corrections.caveats: Run and published by the Oxc project itself. Oxlint and ESLint versions for the published runs are not stated beyond 'ESLint v9'. The repo's package.json now requires eslint ^10, and bench.sh adds an 'eslint --concurrency=auto' run that the README results do not show, so the published numbers predate the current config: VS Code results were last updated 2025-05/09, type-aware results 2025-12. The 50-100x headline applies only to standard rules; with type-aware rules the gain is 8-12x. The Biome comparison uses a single rule. The benchmark repo itself has no LICENSE file (its package.json says MIT).

notes: Tier A stands. The record's claim left out the much lower type-aware results (8.22x and 12.38x) even though its workload lists type-aware rule sets, so I added them to claimed_speedup. Metadata checked: MIT, 22871 stars, last commit 2026-09-24, not a fork.
